How Much Training–Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?

 

Cong Yu 1  Ziting Wang 2  Songlin Jiang 1  Sitong Zhang 3 

Chengliang Chai 4  Youhe Jiang 5  Eiko Yoneki 5  Tuo Shi 6 

1Aalto University  2Nanyang Technological University  3Independent  4Beijing Institute of Technology  5University of Cambridge  6Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology

Abstract

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training–inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student–teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least 1.93× as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality 1.62× sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd/.

1 Introduction

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on responses it samples itself, guided by a fixed teacher that scores every token (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). It brings a stronger or specialized teacher’s ability into the student, and many recent model releases run it as a post-training stage (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026). Its cost lies in producing the responses, called rollouts, which can dominate training time (Kang et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2026). With a standard inference engine in 16-bit BF16, rollout generation and teacher scoring take 76% of each training step’s time on the 7B student (App. Table 11). Therefore, cheaper rollouts mean cheaper OPD.

Two techniques make rollouts cheaper. Quantized inference stores the rollout engine’s weights and key-value (KV) cache in fewer bits, such as the 8-bit FP8 format, so the same GPUs hold more rollouts (Qiu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025b). Asynchronous rollouts let generation run ahead of training, so the trainer does not wait for it, and the rollouts come from weights a few versions old (Fu et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026). However, both come at a price: the rollout engine that generates the rollouts no longer runs exactly the model being trained, so the student learns from responses that are not quite its own. We call this gap mismatch and measure it as the per-token KL divergence between the two models’ next-token distributions, in nats per token. Even a standard engine has a small mismatch, because inference engines and trainers use different kernels and numerics (Liu et al., 2025a; He & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), and quantization and stale weights widen it further.

RL post-training can face the same training–inference mismatch. It also trains a model on its own rollouts, and the mismatch can collapse training (Zhong et al., 2026). Many RL systems therefore correct the update per token (Yao et al., 2025a; Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b). Recent OPD pipelines often apply these remedies (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026).

However, OPD appears far less sensitive to mismatch than RL. Semi-OPD (Zhao et al., 2026) and Lightning OPD (Wu et al., 2026) generate rollouts once, from the untrained student, and distill on them throughout training, so the student drifts away from the rollouts. They still match or beat OPD with fresh rollouts in many settings. AsyncOPD (Kang et al., 2026) lets generation run many batches ahead of training and still reaches the accuracy of synchronous training.

We call this tolerance the mismatch budget: the mismatch OPD can absorb without hurting training, which quantized and asynchronous rollouts can spend on memory and speed. We judge training by held-out KL, the student’s per-token KL to the teacher on held-out problems (§3.2), with accuracy as a second check. Figure 1 shows training accuracy on a 7B student. Inside the budget, FP8 rollouts that keep the first and last layers in BF16 track the standard engine step for step, and rollouts up to 4 versions old train as well as it and finish up to 1.6 times sooner (§5.4). Beyond it, every-layer FP8 rollouts are rarely correct and training fails (§5.1). Whether an engine is safe is decided by the budget, not by its bit width (§5.3): on this student, only quantized engines that keep the first layer’s KV cache in BF16 stay inside the budget.

Measuring this budget and leveraging it is challenging for three reasons. (1) Different sources of mismatch are hard to compare. Quantization is set in bits and asynchrony in versions, and prior OPD studies keep the engine fixed or study staleness alone (Zhao et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a), so no common scale relates the two. (2) Checking an engine costs a training run. A run takes 5.5 to 6 hours on eight GPUs (§5.3), too long to try engines one by one; a useful check should take minutes. (3) Corrections inherited from RL may miss the damage. They act only on the error at each sampled token. Whether that is where mismatch hurts OPD, and whether these corrections widen the budget, has not been tested.

We address these challenges through a measurement study. First, we establish a common mismatch measure to compare different rollout engines, define the mismatch budget, and develop a lightweight admission check to evaluate new configurations without full training runs (§3). Using controlled rollout configurations and evaluation criteria (§4), we characterize OPD’s mismatch tolerance across student models, validate the admission check, and quantify the efficiency gains of cheaper rollouts (§5). Finally, we investigate why OPD behaves differently from RL under mismatch and analyze the errors that per-token corrections may miss (§6).

The study covers three student–teacher pairs from two model families, with 1.5B, 3B and 7B students. Each student is distilled for 200 steps from an RL-fine-tuned version of itself. On the 7B pair, we train 17 rollout configurations (§4.2): six quantized ones from three production recipes, five with different degrees of asynchrony, four with different levels of weight noise, and two combining quantization with asynchrony; the 1.5B and 3B pairs add three and two FP8 runs. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    A methodology for quantifying OPD’s mismatch budget (§3.1, §3.2, §5.1, §5.2). We define a common mismatch measure and a procedure for finding OPD’s mismatch budget. On the 7B student, OPD preserves training quality at over 200 times the standard engine’s mismatch and fails at about twice that level; under the same engines, two RL methods break at about 12 and 60 times. Both mismatch and its effects vary across students.

  • •

    An admission check that takes minutes (§3.3, §5.3, §5.4). Decisions fixed before training matched all eight tested outcomes, five from the offline check, checking six configurations in 24 minutes on one GPU. Within the budget, FP8 KV caches provide at least 1.93 times BF16’s capacity, while FP8 with asynchrony reaches synchronous training’s final held-out KL 1.62 times sooner.

  • •

    An analysis of OPD’s tolerance and its limits (§5.5 and §6). We analyze why OPD tolerates mismatch differently from RL. Mismatch perturbs every OPD update but leaves its goal of matching the teacher unchanged. Its impact grows late in training, and runs beyond the observed budget fail. Under configurations OPD tolerates, uncorrected RL breaks in five of six runs. Per-token corrections can prevent these RL failures but do not improve OPD: the prefix-shift error they cannot address grows 5.3 times from a passing to a failing noise level, versus 2.1 times for per-token error.

2 Background and Motivation

On-policy post-training. RL post-training and OPD are both on-policy: the model learns from responses it samples itself, and both use the same update. The model pθp_{\theta} samples a response yy to a prompt. Each token yty_{t} follows a partial response y<ty_{<t}, its prefix, and receives a score AtA_{t}, its advantage. The update ∑tAt​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(yt∣y<t)\textstyle\sum_{t}A_{t}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) raises the probability of tokens with a positive advantage and lowers it for those with a negative one, so the advantage decides what the model learns.

The two methods differ only in where the advantage comes from. In RL (Williams, 1992; Schulman et al., 2017; Ahmadian et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), it comes from a reward on the whole response, such as whether its final answer is correct, so every token of a response shares one score. OPD (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025) instead lets a fixed teacher pTp_{T} score every token:

At=log⁡pT​(yt∣y<t)−log⁡pθ​(yt∣y<t),A_{t}=\log p_{T}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})-\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}), (1)

which is positive when the teacher finds the token likelier than the student does. Figure 2 shows one training step.

This difference decides where the update vanishes. In RL, a correct response keeps its reward no matter how good the model already is, so each update pushes up the correct responses it sampled. These pushes cancel on average only if responses are sampled exactly as the model would sample them (Williams, 1992); otherwise they leave a net push. In OPD, the advantage is zero at every token once the student matches the teacher, so the update vanishes there, whichever responses it trains on. Before that point, averaged over the student’s own samples, the update lowers KL(pθ∥pT)\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{T}).

Rollouts and mismatch. Rollout generation is a major cost of on-policy training (Kang et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2026), so systems use a rollout engine such as vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). Even with synchronized weights, the engine and trainer can produce slightly different probabilities due to different kernels and numerics (Liu et al., 2025a; He & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Two speedups widen this mismatch. (i) Quantization stores engine weights or KV cache in 8 or 4 bits to fit more responses in memory, while rounding further shifts probabilities (Liu et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026). (ii) Asynchrony overlaps generation and training, so the engine uses weights one or more updates old (Fu et al., 2025; Rang et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026).

Training–inference mismatch also affects RL post-training, where its consequences are better understood. In RL, this mismatch can break training. RL’s update is unbiased only over the model’s own samples, so the engine’s samples skew it regardless of reward. Each weight sync copies this drift back into the engine, where it can accumulate (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b). Even a standard vLLM engine’s small mismatch can make RL training fail, while an exactly matched engine does not (Zhong et al., 2026).

Handling mismatch in RL. RL handles mismatch mainly in two ways. Exact matching gives the engine and trainer shared kernels or a single implementation (He & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Wasti et al., 2025; RadixArk, 2025). It must be rebuilt for each model and GPU type and cannot remove mismatch from quantization with a BF16 trainer or asynchrony. Per-token correction keeps the mismatch and adjusts each sampled token’s update: truncated importance sampling reweights it by a capped probability ratio (Yao et al., 2025a; Yao et al., 2025b), token masks drop it (Ling Team et al., 2025), and score centering removes the drift (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b). These corrections act on sampled tokens, not on which prefixes the engine reaches; for long responses, they cannot bound the error (Li et al., 2025a).

Motivation: mismatch budgets in OPD. OPD pipelines use these corrections as well (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026), but mismatch may affect OPD differently because its update differs from RL’s. As shown above, matching the teacher remains a stationary point whichever engine generates the responses. Mismatch can still change the path to this point and degrade training quality. This raises three questions: (i) How much mismatch can OPD tolerate across different rollout engines and student models? (ii) Can we identify safe rollout configurations before training and use them to reduce rollout costs? (iii) How does mismatch affect OPD’s updates, and can per-token corrections mitigate its effects?

We address these questions by defining a common mismatch measure, an empirical mismatch budget, and a lightweight admission check (§3). Using controlled rollout configurations and evaluation criteria (§4), we measure tolerance, test the admission check, quantify the benefits of cheaper rollouts, and compare OPD with RL (§5). Finally, we analyze update bias and the limits of per-token corrections (§6).

3 Quantifying Mismatch in OPD

Cheaper rollouts benefit OPD only if the mismatch they introduce does not degrade training. To study this trade-off, we measure mismatch on a common scale, determine how much a student tolerates, and estimate the mismatch of new rollout engines before training.

3.1 Measuring Training–Inference Mismatch

Let qq denote the rollout engine’s next-token distribution and pθp_{\theta} the current student distribution used by the trainer. As shown in Figure 2 (top), we measure mismatch between these distributions on the prefixes visited by the engine. They may differ because of inference numerics, quantization, or stale weights. The trainer recomputes the student’s log-probabilities and the advantage in Eq. (1); therefore, the engine changes which tokens and prefixes are used for training, not the advantage assigned to a given token at a given prefix.

At training step nn, we measure mismatch over the NnN_{n} tokens sampled by the engine:

dn=1Nn​∑t[log⁡q⁡(yt∣y<t)−log⁡pθ​(yt∣y<t)].d_{n}=\frac{1}{N_{n}}\sum_{t}\bigl[\log q(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})-\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\bigr]. (2)

This estimates the expected per-token KL(q∥pθ)\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p_{\theta}) over the prefixes visited by the engine, in nats per token. An expected value of zero means the two distributions agree at those prefixes. When rollouts use stale weights, qq is the older model that generated them. Thus, the same measure covers numerical differences, quantization, and staleness.

For a rollout configuration cc, we summarize its training run by the mismatch level D⁡(c)D(c), the average of dnd_{n} over its training steps (steps 1–200 unless a window is stated). In our setup, the standard engine (unmodified vLLM in BF16) has a mismatch of 0.0008 nats/token. This common scale lets us compare engines whose configurations are otherwise expressed in different terms, such as bit width and number of stale model versions.

3.2 Defining the Mismatch Budget

We call the mismatch that OPD can tolerate without a meaningful loss in training quality its mismatch budget. To characterize it, we train the same student with different rollout configurations and compare their outcomes against a standard run using the standard engine.

For a held-out problem xx, let Kx​(c)K_{x}(c) denote the student’s per-token KL to the teacher at the evaluation checkpoint after training with configuration cc, and let Kx​(0)K_{x}(0) denote the corresponding value for the standard run. All students are evaluated using the standard engine, rather than their training rollout engine. We report the mean held-out KL as K⁡(c)=|ℋ|−1​∑x∈ℋKx​(c)K(c)=|\mathcal{H}|^{-1}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{H}}K_{x}(c) over the held-out set ℋ\mathcal{H}. To judge relative degradation, we divide the mean per-problem change in held-out KL by the standard run’s mean:

Δ⁡(c)=∑x∈ℋ(Kx​(c)−Kx​(0))∑x∈ℋKx​(0)=K⁡(c)K⁡(0)−1.\Delta(c)=\frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{H}}\bigl(K_{x}(c)-K_{x}(0)\bigr)}{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{H}}K_{x}(0)}=\frac{K(c)}{K(0)}-1. (3)

A positive Δ⁡(c)\Delta(c) indicates worse agreement with the teacher. We classify a run as failing when Δ⁡(c)\Delta(c) reaches a predefined quality threshold τ\tau and a paired statistical test detects a difference; §4.3 specifies the values and test.

Let 𝒫τ\mathcal{P}_{\tau} and ℱτ\mathcal{F}_{\tau} be the tested runs that pass and fail this rule. When the passing and failing levels are ordered, we characterize the observed transition by an empirical budget bracket:

Bemp​(τ)=[maxc∈𝒫τ⁡D⁡(c),minc∈ℱτ⁡D⁡(c)].B_{\mathrm{emp}}(\tau)=\left[\max_{c\in\mathcal{P}_{\tau}}D(c),\;\min_{c\in\mathcal{F}_{\tau}}D(c)\right]. (4)

Figure 2 (top right) illustrates this bracket: each dot represents a training run that passes or fails the quality rule. The bracket locates the transition in the tested configurations; it does not guarantee that every engine below its upper bound will preserve quality. Its value depends on the student, training setup, and quality threshold.

3.3 Estimating Mismatch Before Training

Locating a budget requires full training runs, but repeating them for every new rollout configuration is expensive. We therefore use a lightweight admission check (Figure 2, bottom) to screen new candidates after a student’s budget has been characterized. A candidate engine cc generates a small set of responses, and the standard BF16 engine re-scores the same tokens using the same student weights. For the MM sampled tokens, we compute

D^​(c)=1M​∑t[log⁡qc​(yt∣y<t)−log⁡q0​(yt∣y<t)],\widehat{D}(c)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{t}\left[\log q_{c}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})-\log q_{0}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})\right], (5)

where qcq_{c} and q0q_{0} are the candidate and standard engines’ token distributions. This is an offline estimate of their per-token difference on the candidate’s visited prefixes. It is only a proxy for D⁡(c)D(c): the standard engine is not numerically identical to the trainer, and mismatch may change as the student trains.

We set an admission line LL using known passing runs and apply a safety margin α>1\alpha>1 to the offline estimate. The admission rule is

admit(c)=[αD^(c)<L].\operatorname{admit}(c)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\alpha\widehat{D}(c)<L\right]. (6)

An admitted configuration is predicted to preserve training quality, not proven safe. The check requires neither teacher scoring nor a full training run for that candidate. Its student-specific budget and admission line still require initial calibration, and we monitor dnd_{n} during training, particularly with stale rollouts. §4.3 gives the check’s experimental settings, and §5.3 evaluates its predictions and limitations.

4 Experimental Setup

Building on the mismatch measure, empirical budget, and admission check introduced in §3, we detail the experimental setup used to evaluate them. We describe the student–teacher pairs, rollout configurations spanning quantization, stale weights, and controlled noise, and the evaluation protocols. We report the results on mismatch tolerance, admission accuracy, and rollout efficiency in §5.

4.1 Training Setup

Models. We consider three student models from two model families, with sizes ranging from 1.5B to 7B parameters. The students are DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (Guo et al., 2025), and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024). Their respective teachers are Skywork-OR1-Math-7B (He et al., 2025b), JustRL-DeepSeek-1.5B (He et al., 2025a), and GT-Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-MATH.

Testbed. Our testbed consists of two nodes, each equipped with four NVIDIA GH200 GPUs. In synchronous runs, one node hosts the teacher, while the other hosts the trainer and four rollout replicas. Asynchronous runs use the same eight GPUs with different placements (App. C.5).

Implementation. We use vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) as the rollout engine and verl (Sheng et al., 2025) for OPD training. Unless stated otherwise, we use neither importance correction nor score centering; both are evaluated in §6.

Training recipe. Each step samples 8 responses per problem for 8 DAPO-Math-17k problems (Yu et al., 2025) at temperature 1, with up to 16,384 tokens per response. The trainer takes one AdamW update per step at learning rate 10−610^{-6}. Each budget run lasts 200 steps.

4.2 Rollout Configurations

On the 7B student, we study OPD’s tolerance to mismatch introduced by practical rollout optimizations (quantization and asynchrony), alone and combined. We also use weight noise to vary mismatch in a controlled manner. For quantized and noisy configurations, we modify only the rollout engine; the trainer, teacher, and checkpoints remain in BF16.

(i) Quantization. We test three recipes: (a) NVIDIA Model Optimizer FP8 (NVIDIA, 2026), which quantizes weights, activations, and KV cache; (b) NVFP4 (Alvarez et al., 2025), which uses 4-bit weights and activations with FP8 KV cache; and (c) vLLM’s FP8 KV cache, which leaves weights and activations in BF16. We test each recipe across all layers and with a variant retaining the first layer’s KV cache in BF16. For Model Optimizer FP8, this variant instead retains the entire first and last layers in BF16. Because NVFP4 requires Blackwell GPUs, we emulate its quantization in BF16 and evaluate quality only, not speed (App. C).

(ii) Stale weights. We vary weight staleness by allowing the rollout engine to use weights up to k∈{1,2,4,8}k\in\{1,2,4,8\} model versions old, using verl’s fully asynchronous mode (meituan-search, 2026). We also test colocated generation and training, where rollouts are at most two versions old (App. C.5).

(iii) Weight noise. After each weight synchronization, we add a fixed Gaussian offset to the rollout engine’s weights, scaled by σ∈{0.0665,0.15,0.234,0.325}\sigma\in\{0.0665,0.15,0.234,0.325\} times each projection matrix’s standard deviation. This provides controlled perturbations along a fixed weight-space direction.

(iv) Combined configurations. We combine Model Optimizer FP8, retaining the first and last layers in BF16, with rollout weights up to four or eight versions old.

4.3 Evaluation and Admission Protocol

We specify how we evaluate training quality, classify rollout configurations for the empirical mismatch budget in §3.2, and calibrate the admission check in §3.3.

Held-out KL evaluation. We evaluate Kx​(c)K_{x}(c) and Δ⁡(c)\Delta(c) on 530 held-out math problems from AIME24 (MAA, 2024) and MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024). At each evaluation checkpoint, responses are generated by the standard BF16 engine; the student and teacher score the same tokens. We compare each configuration with the standard run at the same training step. As defined in Eq. (3), Δ⁡(c)\Delta(c) is the relative change in mean held-out KL; the bootstrap interval resamples problems.

Primary quality rule. We set the quality threshold to τ=0.20\tau=0.20, well above the observed run-to-run variation of at most 1.5% in final held-out KL (§5.1). For scale, standard training on the 7B student reduces mean held-out KL from 0.0965 to 0.0481; a 20% increase in the final value would undo about one fifth of this gain. A configuration fails if Δ⁡(c)≥τ\Delta(c)\geq\tau and the 95% problem-paired bootstrap interval for its KL gap from the standard run excludes zero. The rule was fixed before the runs it evaluates (App. B).

Secondary accuracy rule. We also evaluate mean accuracy on AIME24, AIME25, and the non-overlapping subset of AMC23, using 16 samples per problem at step 200. Accuracy is secondary because OPD optimizes teacher agreement rather than this accuracy measure directly. A run fails this rule if accuracy drops by at least five percentage points and the 95% interval for the difference excludes zero. Typical intervals are about ±2\pm 2 points wide. Only the primary quality rule determines Bemp​(τ)B_{\mathrm{emp}}(\tau).

Admission-check settings. We use three settings for the admission check in §3.3.

(i) Sample size. Each candidate generates two responses for 16 math problems, re-scored by the standard BF16 engine. Across six configurations, 95% interval half-widths are within 30% of the offline estimates.

(ii) Safety margin. A 100-step pilot on the 7B student found in-training mismatch at most 1.47 times the offline estimate (App. F). We thus initially set α=1.5\alpha=1.5.

(iii) Admission line. Two pilot runs of one quantized engine passed the primary quality rule at step 100 at about 0.41 nats/token, so we initially set L=0.41L=0.41 nats/token. We admit a candidate if D^​(c)<L/α≈0.27\widehat{D}(c)<L/\alpha\approx 0.27 nats/token. This is a screening rule, not a quality guarantee (§5.3). Each new student requires budget calibration, and we monitor mismatch during training.

5 Characterizing Mismatch Budgets

Building on the methodology in §3 and setup in §4, we investigate questions (i) and (ii) of §2 and compare OPD with RL: (i) Mismatch tolerance: How much mismatch can OPD tolerate (§5.1–§5.2)? (ii) Admission and efficiency: Can we screen configurations before full training, and what benefits do they provide (§5.3–§5.4)? OPD versus RL: Do configurations tolerated by OPD also preserve RL training quality (§5.5)?

5.1 Quantifying OPD’s Mismatch Budget

We measure the 7B student’s tolerance by training with quantized, stale-weight, and noisy rollout engines and comparing their mismatch D⁡(c)D(c) and held-out KL with standard BF16 under the primary quality rule (§4.3). Figure 3 shows 18 runs of 16 configurations, two run twice; repeated runs differ in final KL by at most 1.5% (App. B.5).

(1) OPD tolerates substantial mismatch (Figure 3; App. Table 6). All twelve configurations with D⁡(c)≤0.184D(c)\leq 0.184 nats/token, over 200 times the standard engine’s D⁡(0)=0.0008D(0)=0.0008, pass with Δ⁡(c)\Delta(c) between −5.0%-5.0\% and +6.4%+6.4\%. Under the same engines, REINFORCE and GRPO break at about 12 and 60 times D⁡(0)D(0) (§5.5). Even the two highest passing levels finish within 0.5% of the standard run’s held-out KL.

(2) Larger mismatch degrades quality (Figure 3; App. Table 6). Both noise runs at D⁡(c)≈0.39D(c)\approx 0.39 fail with Δ⁡(c)≈+23%\Delta(c)\approx+23\%, giving the empirical bracket Bemp​(0.20)=[0.184,0.39]B_{\mathrm{emp}}(0.20)=[0.184,0.39] nats/token, not an exact failure threshold. The three every-layer quantized configurations, with the first layer’s KV cache also in FP8, reach D⁡(c)=0.56D(c)=0.56–0.680.68, fail with Δ⁡(c)=+54%\Delta(c)=+54\%–+60%+60\%, and lose 3–5 accuracy points; under every-layer FP8, rollout answers are almost never correct from the start (Figure 1). The bracket depends on the quality rule: at τ=0.25\tau=0.25 it is [0.39,0.56][0.39,0.56] (App. B.1).

(3) The measure compares different mismatch sources (Figure 3). Passing and failing levels are broadly consistent across quantization and weight noise. Staleness of up to eight versions yields only D⁡(c)=0.0028D(c)=0.0028, far below the failure range. Neither bit width nor staleness alone captures the resulting mismatch.

Insight. A common mismatch measure helps characterize tolerance across rollout optimizations, but the observed budget is specific to the student and quality rule.

5.2 Model-Dependent Mismatch Tolerance

We examine whether the 7B findings transfer to the 1.5B and 3B students by comparing FP8-induced mismatch and training quality. We also vary precision across components on the 7B student. These tests do not establish complete budget brackets for the smaller students.

(1) Similar mismatch need not imply similar quality loss (App. Table 8). Two every-layer FP8 recipes on the 1.5B student yield D⁡(c)=0.36D(c)=0.36–0.390.39 over steps 1–100, versus 0.650.65–0.690.69 for comparable 7B quantization, yet the 1.5B runs finish with Δ⁡(c)=+420%\Delta(c)=+420\% to +479%+479\% and about 11 points lower accuracy; 7B weight-noise runs at a similar mismatch of 0.39 have Δ⁡(c)≈+23%\Delta(c)\approx+23\%. Because both model and mismatch source differ, this comparison does not isolate model tolerance; it argues against transferring the 7B budget without calibration. Keeping the 1.5B student’s first-layer KV cache in BF16 avoids the observed degradation (Δ⁡(c)=−4.3%\Delta(c)=-4.3\%).

(2) FP8 mismatch depends on the model and recipe (Figure 4; App. Table 8). On the 7B student, retaining the first-layer KV cache in BF16 reduces vLLM’s FP8-cache estimate D^​(c)\widehat{D}(c) from 0.52 to 0.0037 nats/token. By contrast, every-layer Model Optimizer FP8 on Llama-3.2-3B yields only D⁡(c)≈0.01D(c)\approx 0.01 and passes (Δ⁡(c)=+5.6%\Delta(c)=+5.6\%). An offline Qwen3-4B check with the score-centering FP8 recipe (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026a) gives D^​(c)=0.005\widehat{D}(c)=0.005 (App. C.2).

(3) Mismatch measurements locate sensitive components (Figure 5). On the 7B student, an FP8 KV cache dominates the mismatch at every tested weight and activation precision, and the first layer’s cache accounts for 93%–99% of it across the seven FP8-cache recipes in Figure 5. The DeepSeek students have a key-projection bias and lack query/key normalization (Henry et al., 2020); on the 7B student, the first layer’s keys are much larger than in most layers. A keys-only emulation attributes about 82% of that layer’s effect to first-layer key rounding (App. C.3). Llama lacks key-projection bias, while Qwen3 normalizes queries and keys, consistent with their lower sensitivity.

Insight. Both the mismatch introduced by a recipe and its quality impact depend on the student; candidate engines therefore require student-specific measurement.

5.3 Evaluating the Admission Check

We compare pre-run mismatch estimates D^​(c)\widehat{D}(c) and admission decisions with full-training outcomes, then assess the check’s cost and pilot-derived parameters (§4.3).

(1) All eight preselected decisions match the observed outcomes (Figure 4; App. Table 8). Of the nine trained configurations in Figure 4, all eight with decisions fixed before full training, five from the offline check, match the primary quality rule. On the 7B student, retaining first-layer BF16 KV cache passes while quantizing it to FP8 fails; offline estimates fall at D^​(c)≤0.030\widehat{D}(c)\leq 0.030 or ≥0.408\geq 0.408. The boundary L/α≈0.27L/\alpha\approx 0.27 lies between these groups, so the check is untested near the boundary.

(2) Screening is inexpensive after calibration. Checking six configurations takes 24 minutes on one GPU, versus 5.5 to 6 hours on eight GPUs for one full training run. The check requires neither trainer nor teacher, but the initial student-specific budget calibration still requires representative training runs.

(3) Pilot-based safety settings can be insufficient (App. Table 8). During training, the admitted 7B engines reach 1.56–1.68 times their estimates (steps 1–100), exceeding the pilot margin α=1.5\alpha=1.5. Noise at D⁡(c)=0.39D(c)=0.39 fails at step 200 despite lying below the pilot admission line L=0.41L=0.41. Retrospectively setting L=0.184L=0.184 would preserve all eight tested decisions with a more conservative boundary, but does not establish general safety.

Insight. Offline estimates support low-cost screening, provided the admission line and margin are calibrated conservatively and mismatch is monitored during training.

5.4 Efficiency Within the Budget

We measure throughput, KV-cache capacity, and time-to-quality on the 7B student using quality-preserving rollout configurations. Throughput is optimizer updates per hour relative to synchronous BF16, excluding warm-up and asynchronous drain-only steps (App. B.3). We also benchmark a separate memory-bound batch.

(1) Asynchrony helps until the trainer becomes the bottleneck (Figure 6; App. Table 8). Throughput rises with staleness kk and levels off at 1.62×1.62\times and 1.59×1.59\times for k=4k=4 and 8; all runs pass and finish within 3% of the standard held-out KL. In synchronous training, the trainer waits for rollouts and teacher scores (App. Figure 11); from k=2k=2 on, this wait is at most three seconds, and training limits throughput to about 55 updates/hour. FP8 combined with k=4,8k=4,8 gives 1.63×1.63\times and 1.55×1.55\times, close to asynchrony alone, because generation is off the critical path.

(2) FP8 weights improve speed; FP8 KV cache mainly adds capacity (Figure 7; App. Tables 11 and 11). At 64 responses/step, Model Optimizer FP8 with BF16 first/last layers speeds up generation and raises updates/hour by 1.27×1.27\times; vLLM’s FP8 cache alone gives 1.00×1.00\times (App. Table 11). FP8 holds at least 1.93×1.93\times as many KV-cache tokens on the 7B student, but BF16 does not exhaust its cache at this batch size. At 1,536 responses/step, BF16 runs out of cache and must evict and recompute running responses, while FP8 does not. vLLM’s FP8 cache and Model Optimizer FP8 then give 1.11×1.11\times and 1.16×1.16\times throughput, respectively. The latter gain is smaller than at the training batch because generation and teacher scoring take only 42% of each step (App. E).

(3) Cheaper rollouts reach the same quality sooner (App. Table 11). We measure wall-clock time from the first training step to the synchronous standard run’s step-200 held-out KL, including generation, teacher scoring, and checkpoint saves. Model Optimizer FP8 with k=8k=8 reaches this target 1.62×1.62\times sooner, with final accuracy 60.5% versus 61.5%. A second preselected target, 90% of the standard run’s KL improvement, gives the same speedup; with FP8 and k=4k=4, it is reached 1.69×1.69\times sooner and final KL stays within 0.8% of the standard run.

Insight. Asynchrony removes rollout waiting, while FP8 benefits depend on whether generation speed or KV-cache capacity limits the workload. All these 200-step runs pass the primary rule with D⁡(c)≤0.013D(c)\leq 0.013 nats/token.

5.5 RL Breaks Where OPD Holds

We test whether configurations tolerated by OPD also preserve RL training quality by comparing GRPO and REINFORCE with their respective standard-engine baselines (Figure 8); prior work reports RL mismatch sensitivity (Zhong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025a).

Setup.

Both RL methods train the 7B student with a 0/1 reward for a correct boxed answer, without a teacher. Following a scaled-down JustRL recipe (He et al., 2025a), each step uses 16 problems and eight responses per problem, learning rate 10−610^{-6}, and no KL penalty or importance correction. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) normalizes within each group and takes two updates per step; REINFORCE (Williams, 1992; Ahmadian et al., 2024) uses raw reward. Each method runs 200 steps with four OPD rollout configurations and its own standard engine. A run breaks if held-out DAPO accuracy on 1,000 problems drops at least five points, or if entropy or response length collapses with held-out confirmation. These criteria were fixed in advance. Neither standard RL run improves held-out accuracy measurably by step 100, so we assess failure rather than learning gains (App. B.2).

(1) REINFORCE breaks under all three OPD-passing configurations (Figure 8). With weight noise at 0.097 (σ=0.15\sigma=0.15), its reward reaches zero and held-out accuracy falls 21 points by step 200. With NVFP4 and first-layer BF16 KV cache, responses hit the length limit and accuracy falls 59 points. With FP8 keeping the first and last layers in BF16, reward nearly vanishes and accuracy falls 63 points.

(2) GRPO breaks under two of the three (Figure 8). Noise and NVFP4 break it, but FP8 with BF16 first and last layers passes. With NVFP4, entropy collapses and accuracy falls 15 points; with noise, more held-out answers hit the length limit. Every-layer FP8 breaks all methods, including OPD.

(3) Initial mismatch and early weight changes do not explain the contrast. RL runs start at 0.88–1.02 times the matching OPD runs’ mismatch and move weights only 0.43–0.90 times as far as OPD’s standard run in the first 100 steps.

(4) Score centering prevents the tested RL failures (App. B.2). Under one engine per method, score centering (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b) raises REINFORCE’s held-out accuracy by 61 points at step 100 and GRPO’s by 16.5 points at step 200. A control that computes but does not apply centering still breaks.

Insight. The tested RL failures do not predict OPD’s tolerance. We examine this contrast and the limits of per-token corrections in §6.

6 Discussion

OPD’s target explains part of its tolerance; the drift’s sign does not. Per-token corrections do not help OPD, and under weight noise part of the error comes from the prefixes (partial responses) that the engine reaches.

(1) The error vanishes at the teacher. At one prefix, let δ=q−pθ\delta=q-p_{\theta} be the engine’s deviation and A=log⁡pT−log⁡pθA=\log p_{T}-\log p_{\theta} the teacher–student log ratio over the vocabulary. In the gradient with respect to the logits zz, mismatch adds

gbiasz=δ⊙A−pθ​(δ⊤​A),‖gbiasz‖1≤2​‖δ‖1​‖A‖∞.\begin{gathered}g^{z}_{\mathrm{bias}}=\delta\odot A-p_{\theta}\,(\delta^{\top}A),\\ \bigl\|g^{z}_{\mathrm{bias}}\bigr\|_{1}\leq 2\,\|\delta\|_{1}\,\|A\|_{\infty}.\end{gathered} (7)

It vanishes as the student approaches the teacher, whatever the engine. With a constant reward RR in place of AA, as in REINFORCE, the error is R​δR\,\delta, which need not shrink. With the engine fixed, the expected OPD gradient is exactly that of 12​𝔼q​[(log⁡pθ−log⁡pT)2]\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{q}[(\log p_{\theta}-\log p_{T})^{2}] (App. D.2), so matching the teacher stays a stationary point whatever the engine. This needs the advantage computed from the trainer’s log-probabilities, not the engine’s.

(2) During training, the error shrinks, but the update shrinks faster. At three weight-noise levels on fixed prefixes, the error of Eq. (7) at step 200 is 0.11 to 0.13 of its size at the untrained student. The update itself shrinks faster: at the middle level, the error-to-update ratio is 0.93 at the untrained student and 1.88 at step 200 (App. D). So mismatch matters more, not less, late in training.

(3) The drift’s sign does not protect OPD. Under weight noise, the student moves away from the engine, as OPD’s negative drift coefficient (the mean advantage under the engine) predicts (App. B.1). Adding a constant bb to every advantage keeps the expected on-policy update but shifts the coefficient by bb. With b=+0.15b=+0.15 and +0.5+0.5 under noise at mismatch 0.097, the coefficient turns positive, as in REINFORCE, and the student moves toward the engine, but held-out KL ends 6.5% and 6.9% below the standard run’s (App. Table H).

(4) Neither tested correction helps OPD. Score centering (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b) removes the drift, but under noise at mismatch 0.055 and 0.097 it leaves held-out KL 2.3% to 3.7% above uncentered OPD’s. At 0.097, truncated importance sampling raises held-out KL by 2.9% and 7.0% at steps 100 and 200, and FP8 on every layer still fails.

(5) Part of the error comes from the prefixes the engine reaches. We split the update’s error into two parts (Figure 9; App. D.3): TT, the per-token error, from the engine’s different next-token probabilities at the prefixes it visits, and SS, the prefix shift, from visiting different prefixes than the standard engine. Both parts grow from a passing noise level (0.097, σ=0.15\sigma=0.15) to the failing one (0.39, σ=0.325\sigma=0.325). At the untrained student, SS grows more: 5.3 times against 2.1 in our main split, and more in every way of splitting. Per-token corrections act only on TT. Only reweighting whole responses reaches SS, and by our estimate that needs about 102710^{27} responses per effective sample even at our smallest noise (App. D.1), so keeping mismatch inside the budget remains the practical remedy.

(6) Offline OPD sits inside the budget. Semi-OPD and Lightning OPD (Zhao et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026) draw rollouts once from the untrained student and rescore them with the current student, in effect using a rollout engine with fixed weights. Neither paper reports a KL mismatch. On 7B standard-run checkpoints it is 0.082 nats/token at steps 100 and 200, below the bracket’s lower end of 0.184 (App. C.5).

7 Related Work

Cheaper rollouts. Quantized rollouts reduce memory costs but introduce training–inference mismatch. Prior RL work explores update correction, shared low-precision execution, and quantization-aware approaches (Liu et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Xi et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026). KV-cache quantizers preserve sensitive tokens or outliers (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024), while asynchronous RL overlaps generation and learning at the cost of stale weights (Fu et al., 2025; verl-project, 2026; Hu et al., 2026). Zheng et al. (2025) factor one importance weight into mismatch and staleness. We compare how quantization, staleness, and controlled weight noise affect OPD training quality.

Removing mismatch. Exact-matching approaches align rollout and training execution through shared or deterministic kernels and unified execution (He & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Wasti et al., 2025; RadixArk, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Jiang & SkyRL Team, 2026; Bai & Shen, 2026). Routing replay similarly aligns expert choices in mixture-of-experts models (Ma et al., 2026). Such approaches address execution-induced mismatch, whereas quantizing only the rollout engine or using stale weights introduces mismatch by design. Rather than requiring exact agreement, this study measures how much mismatch OPD can tolerate.

Correcting the update in RL. RL systems mitigate mismatch through importance weighting (Yao et al., 2025a; Yao et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), token or response masking (Liu et al., 2025a; Luo et al., 2026; Ling Team et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), and score centering, which removes mismatch-induced drift (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b) (App. B.1). Other approaches penalize policy divergence (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026), while prior work identifies limits of per-token corrections on long responses (Li et al., 2025a). Production OPD pipelines also adopt RL-style corrections (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2026). In tested OPD runs, neither truncated importance sampling nor score centering helps; under weight noise, per-token corrections cannot address prefix shifts (Section 6).

Distillation on stale or fixed rollouts. Near-Policy, AsyncOPD, and ff-OPD study OPD with stale rollouts (Rang et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a): AsyncOPD examines KL objectives, while ff-OPD regulates stale-sample influence. Semi-OPD and Lightning OPD instead reuse rollouts sampled once from the initial student (Zhao et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Low-bit OPD distills a quantized student (Chen et al., 2026b), whereas here the student remains in BF16 and only the rollout engine is quantized. Complementing these methods, this study measures OPD’s tolerance across mismatch sources and uses a calibrated budget to screen rollout configurations before training.

8 Conclusion

This paper examined the trade-off between rollout efficiency and training quality under training–inference mismatch in OPD. OPD tolerates mismatch that destabilizes RL, but safe ranges depend on the model and cannot be inferred from bit width or staleness alone. On the 7B student, OPD keeps its training quality up to more than 200 times a standard engine’s mismatch, while two RL methods break at about 12 and 60 times. Under weight noise, part of OPD’s error comes from the partial responses the engine reaches, a prefix shift that per-token corrections cannot fix. Calibrated budgets and an admission check help select FP8 and asynchronous configurations that preserve quality, increasing KV-cache capacity and reaching the same held-out KL target 1.62 times sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Overall, mismatch budgets offer a practical basis for balancing rollout efficiency and training quality in OPD. In practice, a few training runs calibrate a student’s budget; the admission check then screens new engines in minutes, and logging mismatch throughout training catches any later drift beyond the offline estimate.

Appendix

Appendix A About This Appendix

This appendix accompanies the main paper, on how much training–inference mismatch on-policy distillation (OPD) tolerates and what speed that buys. Sections 1–8, Figures 1–9 and Equations (1)–(7) are in the main paper; citations refer to its reference list.

Terms.

  • •

    Students. Our 7B student, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, has Skywork-OR1-Math-7B as its teacher; the smaller students are DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Section 4).

  • •

    Rollout engine, trainer. The engine (vLLM) generates the training responses from a copy of the student; the trainer updates the student. Our engines differ from the trainer by quantization, stale weights (asynchronous rollouts) or weight noise.

  • •

    Standard engine, standard run. The standard engine is vLLM in BF16 with the trainer’s current weights; the standard run trains with it.

  • •

    Mismatch. Per-token KL from the engine’s next-token distribution to the trainer’s, on the engine’s tokens, in nats/token (Eq. (2)); a run’s level is its mean over steps (standard engine: 0.0008).

  • •

    Held-out KL. The student’s per-token KL to the teacher on 530 held-out math problems, with standard-engine responses, in nats/token; verdicts use its change relative to the standard run at the same step.

  • •

    Primary rule, budget. A run fails if its held-out KL is 20% or more above the standard run’s and the 95% interval excludes zero (App. B.1). The budget lies between the highest passing and lowest failing levels: 0.184 to 0.39 nats/token on our 7B student.

  • •

    Admission check. An offline mismatch estimate before training; an engine is admitted if 1.5 times the estimate is below 0.41 nats/token, a line set from the pilot that later proved too high (Section 4.3).

  • •

    Draft head. The 7B pair’s training rollouts use an EAGLE-3 draft head for speculative decoding, which leaves the engine’s distribution unchanged (App. G).

Contents.

App. B: pre-registered rules; C: rollout engines; D: gradient probe; E: speed benchmark; F: the 100-step pilot; G: reproducibility; H: result tables; I: limitations.

Appendix B Pre-registration

This appendix gives the rules behind the main text’s verdicts. Each experiment entered a dated, append-only plan before its jobs ran, except the 30-step check without the draft head (Table 11).

B.1 Rules for the OPD runs

These rules judge every OPD run; their verdicts place the budget of Section 5.1.

Reference and mismatch.

Each OPD run is compared with a standard run sharing its seed, data order and recipe. At step 200 this is the 200-step standard run; at step 100, the mean of three earlier 100-step standard runs. Where a plan fixed the step-100 reading as the verdict before training was extended to 200 steps, both readings are reported. The two references differ by 0.04% in held-out KL at step 100. The staleness runs (App. C.5) use the 200-step run at both steps. A run’s mismatch DD is verl’s per-step estimate of KL(q∥p)\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p) (Eq. (2)), averaged over the steps before the checkpoint being read.

Primary rule: held-out KL.

Each checkpoint samples responses with a standard engine (8 per AIME24 problem, 1 per MATH-500 problem), which are teacher-forced through the checkpoint and the teacher. KLx\mathrm{KL}_{x} is the mean of log⁡pθ​(yt)−log⁡pT​(yt)\log p_{\theta}(y_{t})-\log p_{T}(y_{t}) over problem xx’s response tokens, with AIME24’s 8 samples pooled. With rel=(KLxrun−KLxref)¯/KLxref¯\mathrm{rel}=\overline{(\mathrm{KL}^{\mathrm{run}}_{x}-\mathrm{KL}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{x})}\,/\,\overline{\mathrm{KL}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{x}} over the 530 problems, a run fails if rel≥+20%\mathrm{rel}\geq+20\% and the 95% percentile interval of the mean difference, from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of problems, excludes zero.

Accuracy composite (secondary).

The composite averages AIME24, AIME25 (30 problems each) and the 28 of AMC23’s 83 problems that a text-overlap rule does not flag as overlapping the training pool. A run fails if it is at least 5 points below the reference’s with a problem-paired 95% interval excluding zero.

How the budget depends on the 20% line.

Any line from 6.4% to 23.3% gives the same bracket, [0.184, 0.39] (Table 1). The accuracy rule is coarser: its intervals are about ±2\pm 2 points wide (for the runs at 0.39, −0.66-0.66 [−2.80-2.80, +1.50+1.50] and −1.41-1.41 [−3.46-3.46, +0.71+0.71]).

Collapse rule.

The trainer’s entropy, the response length or the length-cap rate collapses if its 5-step rolling mean, minus its mean over the run’s first 10 steps, stays outside its band, [m−R,m+R][m-R,\,m+R], for at least 5 consecutive steps, with RR and mm the range and midpoint of the same difference in the reference run.

Drift tests (weight-noise runs).

These tests ask whether the weights move toward or away from the noisy engine. A checkpoint’s displacement at step ss along a unit direction uu, relative to the reference run, is

Xs​(u)=⟨θsrun−θsref,u⟩,X_{s}(u)=\bigl\langle\theta_{s}^{\mathrm{run}}-\theta_{s}^{\mathrm{ref}},\,u\bigr\rangle, (8)

with n^\hat{n} the direction of the engine’s weight offset (Xs​(n^)>0X_{s}(\hat{n})>0: toward the engine) and u1,…,u200u_{1},\dots,u_{200} random directions (App. C.4). It is specific if |X⁡(n^)||X(\hat{n})| at step 200 exceeds the 97.5th percentile of |X⁡(uk)||X(u_{k})|, and has leveled off if also specific at step 100 with an increment to step 200 under half the step-100 value. The first runs at σ=0.0665\sigma=0.0665, 0.15 and 0.325 read specific, away from the engine, and leveled off (Section 6).

Score centering and the advantage offset.

Score centering (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b) replaces the score ∇log⁡pθ​(y)\nabla\log p_{\theta}(y) by its difference from the engine’s expected score, which removes the drift term: the mean advantage under the engine, A¯q\bar{A}_{q}, times the engine’s mean score (Section 6). For OPD, A¯q=KL(q∥pθ)−KL(q∥pT)\bar{A}_{q}=\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p_{\theta})-\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p_{T}), negative while the engine is closer to the student than to the teacher; its token means under weight noise are in Table 5.

The advantage offset adds a constant bb to every response token’s advantage, which shifts the drift coefficient by bb under mismatch (Section 6). The runs use b=±0.15b=\pm 0.15 and b=+0.5b=+0.5; a positive offset is predicted to move the student toward the engine.

B.2 Rules for the GRPO and REINFORCE comparison

These rules judge the GRPO and REINFORCE runs of Section 5.5.

Recipe and learning test.

The problems are those of DAPO-Math-17k (Yu et al., 2025) on which the untrained student solved 1 to 7 of 8 samples; GRPO’s second update per step clips the probability ratio to [0.8,1.28][0.8,1.28]. The plan first required each method to pass a learning test with the standard engine (among its criteria, a held-out accuracy gain larger than the run-to-run spread). In one run each at a learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, both stayed healthy at steps 100 and 200 but did not pass. The condition was dropped after those runs were read and before any run under mismatch.

Breakage, judged the same way for every method.

Against its own method’s standard run, a run is broken by a held-out accuracy drop of at least 5 points with a problem-paired interval excluding zero and larger than the plan’s run-to-run margin, an entropy or length collapse confirmed on held-out samples, a non-finite loss or, for OPD, the primary rule. It is collapsed if, in addition, its reward is zero for five steps in a row, its responses stay at the length limit, or its entropy falls below half its standard-engine level.

Score centering at one engine per method.

At one engine where each method broke, it was trained twice more: with score centering over the engine’s 128 (REINFORCE) or 256 (GRPO) most likely tokens, and with a control that computes the centering term without applying it. By rules fixed in advance, centering rescues a run if the centered run shows none of the uncorrected run’s failures, and the rescue is due to centering if the control still shows them. One run per side.

REINFORCE, with Model Optimizer’s FP8 recipe and the first and last layers in BF16: the run without corrections lost held-out accuracy and its reward fell below a band built as in the collapse rule (App. B.1) from REINFORCE’s standard run. The control shows both failures, the centered run neither; its held-out accuracy is +60.98 points [+58.67, +63.32] above the uncorrected run’s at step 100.

GRPO, with NVFP4 (emulated) and the first layer’s KV cache in BF16: the run without corrections failed only by an entropy collapse (below its band from step 29, below half its standard-run level from step 72), which the control shows and the centered run does not. Against the run without corrections, the centered run is level at step 100 (−0.15-0.15 points [−1.62-1.62, +1.35+1.35]), so the rules’ stricter label, a rescue at no accuracy cost, is missed by 0.025 points; it is +16.50 points [+14.70, +18.32] higher at step 200.

B.3 Speed readings

These rules produce the speed numbers of Section 5.4. They give no speed or memory number for an emulated format and, as first written, no claim that quantization makes a step faster.

  • •

    Throughput. Updates per hour from step 3, relative to the synchronous standard run on the same GPUs; an asynchronous run’s final steps, which only finish rollouts already in flight, are left out.

  • •

    Large rollout batch. Eight-step runs at 1,024 and 1,536 sequences per step, with no quality claim; a memory-saving gain in updates per hour is credited only at 1,536 and only to vLLM’s FP8 cache with the first layer’s KV cache in BF16.

  • •

    Time to quality. The combined run uses Model Optimizer’s FP8 recipe with the first and last layers in BF16 and the largest staleness whose run passes the primary rule at step 100 (8 versions). It and the synchronous standard run save checkpoints every 25 steps; the targets are the latter’s step-200 held-out KL and 90% of its improvement from step 0 to step 200.

B.4 Admission predictions

These predictions, fixed before training against the admission line of 0.41 nats/token, form the record of Table 8 (Section 5.3). Eight held, and a forecast that vLLM’s FP8 cache at its default scale on every layer fails was hit. For every admitted engine, 1.5 times its estimate is at most 0.045; for every rejected one, at least 0.61. So any line in between, including the lower end of our 7B student’s budget, 0.184, gives the same record.

B.5 One run per configuration

Each configuration is trained once, except four trained twice, so every verdict is provisional; each pair is reported as a range, never pooled. Repeats of the standard and combined runs, which only save checkpoints more often, end at step 200 at a held-out KL of 0.047643 against 0.048103 (1.0% lower) and 0.047602 against 0.048322 (1.5% lower). Repeats at 0.097 and 0.39 nats/token with a second rollout seed differ from their first runs by under 1 point of relative held-out KL at steps 100 and 200. The synchronous standard run took 5.8 and 6.0 hours in two runs, the second saving six more checkpoints.

B.6 Experiments and their status

Table 2 lists every experiment; training runs last 200 steps unless stated.

B.7 Decisions made with data in hand

These decisions, taken with data in hand, change what the paper reports.

  • •

    The pilot. The study’s hypotheses, its 200-step length, its production recipes and four constants (the offset’s size, the admission line and its safety margin, the largest noise level) were chosen with a 100-step pilot’s data (App. F).

  • •

    GRPO and REINFORCE. The learning condition was dropped after the standard runs were read; the engines were chosen after OPD’s results at them, and the noise level after REINFORCE collapsed at it under an earlier recipe.

  • •

    Later runs. After the fifteen original runs of Table 6 were read, we added second runs at 0.097 and 0.39, a level at 0.184 nats/token, and the correction, prefix-shift and first-layer measurements, each with readings fixed before its jobs, except that the first-layer predictions knew an earlier, unrecorded measurement and one correction check was loosened from a relative error of 10−410^{-4} to 10−310^{-3} after data.

  • •

    Readings fixed after some data. The admission record’s window (steps 1–100) was fixed after the first Model Optimizer run’s data; steps 1–200 give the same verdicts. The drift test’s leveling-off reading was fixed knowing the values at σ=0.15\sigma=0.15, before the other two runs were read. The 1,536-sequence set was added after the benchmark without training, before the first large-batch set started.

  • •

    The combined run’s engine was changed before the run from the every-layer FP8 recipe, which the offline estimates put outside the budget, to the same recipe with the first and last layers in BF16.

  • •

    The check without the draft head was added after every other speed result was read. By the authors’ decision after its data, its Model Optimizer FP8 result is reported as a gain in updates per hour at the training batch, which the plan had excluded.

  • •

    The run with weights up to 4 versions old and FP8 was added after the 8-version run’s time to quality was known; it ends 0.8% above the synchronous run’s final held-out KL, so Section 5.4 reports its time to the 90% target.

Appendix C Rollout Engines

This appendix defines the rollout engines of Section 4.2 and the offline estimate of Section 4.3.

C.1 Quantized rollout engines

Table 3 lists the quantized engines of Sections 5.1 and 5.3: Model Optimizer’s recipes (NVIDIA, 2026) and the FP8 attention cache of vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). FP8 is E4M3 throughout.

Emulated formats.

NVFP4 (Alvarez et al., 2025) needs Blackwell GPUs, so it is emulated: tensors are rounded to its grid with Model Optimizer’s scales and used in BF16, checked bit for bit against Model Optimizer’s fake quantization on 21 captured layers. Emulated formats give mismatch and quality only.

Calibration set.

Calibrated scales come from 512 untrained-student responses (temperature 1) to 256 DAPO-Math-17k training problems (seed 20261008), disjoint from all held-out and evaluation sets. Activation and cache scales stay fixed; new weights are re-quantized at every sync.

The default FP8 cache.

Without cache scales in the checkpoint, vLLM stores the cache in FP8 at scale 1, coarse for the 7B student’s large first-layer keys (per-head RMS 10 to 43). A vLLM option keeps listed layers’ cache in BF16.

C.2 Offline estimate of the mismatch

The offline estimate runs on one GPU before training. The engine under test samples 2 responses to each of 16 prompts (problems 0–7 of AIME24 and of MATH-500; temperature 1, top-pp 1, up to 16,384 tokens, seed 777). The estimate is the mismatch of Eq. (2) on these tokens, with the standard engine in place of the student’s pθp_{\theta} and a 95% bootstrap interval over prompts. The standard engine against itself gives 0.00057 [0.00044, 0.00070] nats/token.

First-layer share.

To test whether the first layer dominates on another family (Section 5.3), the share (A−B)/(A−F)(A-B)/(A-F) compares the full recipe (AA), the recipe with the first layer’s KV cache in BF16 (BB) and the standard engine (FF). On Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025), the score-centering code’s FP8 recipe (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026a) (emulated) gives 0.0048 [0.0032, 0.0074] nats/token and a share of −0.18-0.18 [−0.97-0.97, 0.36], against 0.515 and 0.968 for the same recipe on the 7B student.

C.3 Why the first layer’s keys carry the mismatch

This measurement on the untrained 7B student finds which first-layer tensor carries the FP8 cache’s mismatch (Section 5.3). Table 4 gives the offline estimate, the only unit compared with the budget, and the exact KL at the 1,024 fixed prefixes of App. C.5.

The keys carry it.

Alone, the first layer’s keys give 82.5% [73.7, 91.4] of the keys-and-values offline estimate.

Why keys, not queries.

The first layer’s keys share a large common component, so FP8 adds a different error to each score in a query’s row of attention scores. A query’s error, multiplied by these nearly alike keys, shifts that whole row almost equally, which the softmax ignores. Rounding the queries, as vLLM does, has 4.9% of the keys’ effect on the attention weights.

The real kernel.

A tensor-level check confirmed bit for bit that vLLM’s FP8 cache rounds these tensors as the emulation does.

Missed predictions.

Extra mantissa bits for the keys lower the KL more steeply than predicted, and no measure we computed ranks the four first-layer key–value heads as their KL does.

C.4 Rollout engine with weight noise

Construction.

At each weight sync the engine adds σ​sw​εw\sigma s_{w}\varepsilon_{w} to each of the 196 projection matrices WW in the transformer blocks; sws_{w} is the standard deviation of WW at the first sync, and εw∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\varepsilon_{w}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) is seeded by a hash of seed 20261001 and the matrix’s name ww. The offset n=(σ​sw​εw)wn=(\sigma s_{w}\varepsilon_{w})_{w} is thus fixed across syncs and replicas, and unseen by the trainer.

Direction.

The unit direction n^=n/‖n‖\hat{n}=n/\|n\| does not depend on σ\sigma; the 200 random directions of App. B.1 use seeds 1 to 200 instead, with the same sws_{w}.

Levels.

The levels σ=0.0665\sigma=0.0665, 0.15 and 0.325 ran at 0.055, 0.097 and 0.39 nats/token (Table 6). The level σ=0.234\sigma=0.234 was added after the other runs had been read, to fall between the passing and failing levels; it ran at 0.184 and ended 0.5% better at step 200, against a predicted 3% to 12% worse.

C.5 Staleness

This subsection defines the stale-weight engines (Sections 5.1 and 5.4) and one never refreshed (Section 6).

Fully asynchronous runs.

Rollout and training use separate GPUs; responses may be up to k∈{1,2,4,8}k\in\{1,2,4,8\} versions older than the trainer. All kk share one split of the synchronous reference’s total GPUs: the trainer on two of the student node’s four, two rollout replicas on the other two, and the teacher’s four replicas on a second node. With no run at k=0k=0, the k=1k=1 run shows the asynchronous machinery’s cost.

Colocated run.

Trainer and rollout share the GPUs. After one warm-up batch, a token is trained only if it is at most two weight versions old. A step starts once 8 of the 16 prompt groups in flight finish; interrupted generations resume under the new weights.

An engine whose weights are never refreshed.

Semi-OPD (Zhao et al., 2026) and Lightning OPD (Wu et al., 2026) rescore rollouts drawn once from the untrained student with the current student, without importance weights. Their mismatch at step nn is the student’s change since step 0, KL(pθ0∥pθn)\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta_{0}}\,\|\,p_{\theta_{n}}), computed exactly on the 1,024 fixed prefixes of Section 6: 16 uniform positions in one untrained-student response to each of 64 held-out problems (temperature 1, capped at 4,096 tokens). It is 0.082 nats/token at steps 100 and 200; the checkpoints come from standard runs, and a student trained on fixed rollouts may change differently.

Appendix D The Gradient Probe

This appendix holds the analyses behind the discussion of why OPD tolerates mismatch (Section 6).

Setup.

At the untrained student, the probe computes exactly the expected loss gradient of OPD (the negative of the update of Section 2, so Gbias=−gbiaszG_{\mathrm{bias}}=-g^{z}_{\mathrm{bias}} of Eq. (7)) with the advantage of Eq. (1) under the weight-noise engines at σ=0.0665\sigma=0.0665 and 0.15, and its drift part (GdriftG_{\mathrm{drift}} below). At a prefix, pp, pTp_{T} and qq are the student’s, teacher’s and engine’s next-token distributions, zz the student’s logits and Av=log⁡pT​(v)−log⁡pvA_{v}=\log p_{T}(v)-\log p_{v}. Token yy’s loss ℓ⁡(y)=−Ay​log⁡py\ell(y)=-A_{y}\log p_{y}, with AyA_{y} fixed, has ∇zℓ​(y)=−Ay​(ey−p)\nabla_{z}\ell(y)=-A_{y}(e_{y}-p) (eye_{y} one-hot; ∘\circ, ⋅\cdot: element-wise and inner products):

GKL\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{KL}} =Ey∼p​∇zℓ​(y)=−(p∘A−(p⋅A)​p),\displaystyle=\mathrm{E}_{y\sim p}\,\nabla_{z}\ell(y)=-\bigl(p\circ A-(p\cdot A)\,p\bigr), (9)
Gq\displaystyle G_{q} =Ey∼q​∇zℓ​(y)=−(q∘A−(q⋅A)​p),\displaystyle=\mathrm{E}_{y\sim q}\,\nabla_{z}\ell(y)=-\bigl(q\circ A-(q\cdot A)\,p\bigr),
Gbias\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{bias}} =Gq−GKL,\displaystyle=G_{q}-G_{\mathrm{KL}},
Gdrift\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{drift}} =−(q⋅A)​(q−p).\displaystyle=-(q\cdot A)\,(q-p).

GKL=∇zKL(p∥pT)G_{\mathrm{KL}}=\nabla_{z}\mathrm{KL}(p\|p_{T}) is the on-policy target, GbiasG_{\mathrm{bias}} what the engine adds, and GdriftG_{\mathrm{drift}} the part score centering removes (Marek & Ryabinin, 2026b). Backpropagating ⟨stopgrad⁡(Gt),zt⟩\langle\mathrm{stopgrad}(G_{t}),z_{t}\rangle, averaged over response tokens tt, gives each GG’s parameter gradient gg; gq=gKL+gbiasg_{q}=g_{\mathrm{KL}}+g_{\mathrm{bias}}, rbias=‖gbias‖/‖gKL‖r_{\mathrm{bias}}=\|g_{\mathrm{bias}}\|/\|g_{\mathrm{KL}}\|, and n^\hat{n} is the unit direction of the noisy engine’s weight offset (App. C.4).

The prefixes are all positions of 64 responses of the untrained student (442,792 tokens); qq enters only through the next-token distributions. The closed form matches autograd (relative error 5.2×10−55.2\times 10^{-5} in fp32).

Reading.

The mismatched update points in nearly the right direction (Table 5): at σ=0.0665\sigma=0.0665 and 0.15 the bias is 8% and 27% of ‖gKL‖\|g_{\mathrm{KL}}\|, and gqg_{q} lies within 4.2 and 12.2 degrees of gKLg_{\mathrm{KL}}. The bias projects positively on n^\hat{n}, so a gradient step moves the student away from the engine along n^\hat{n}, as a negative drift coefficient Eq​[A]\mathrm{E}_{q}[A] predicts.

The error at later checkpoints.

The error shrinks in training; the update shrinks faster. On the 1,024 fixed prefixes of App. C.5, each checkpoint’s engine adds weight noise scaled to a mismatch of 0.05, 0.2 or 0.4 nats/token (within 10%). The reading fixed in advance is the ratio of the error of Eq. (7) (summed per-prefix norm) at step 200 of the standard run to that at the untrained student: 0.130 [0.108, 0.153], 0.130 [0.110, 0.151] and 0.109 [0.094, 0.126] (95% bootstrap intervals over problems). At a mismatch of 0.2, the error-to-update ratio (rbiasr_{\mathrm{bias}} on 64 prefixes, a descriptive reading) is 0.93 at the untrained student and 1.88 at step 200.

D.1 Corrections at a fixed prefix

This subsection tests whether per-token corrections, which did not help OPD in training (Section 6), reduce the error at a fixed prefix, and what reweighting whole responses costs.

Measurement.

For tokens drawn from the engine, we compare five per-token estimators with the exact on-policy update: plain OPD, score centering (exact, and on the engine’s top 128 tokens as in our runs), and importance weights pθ/qp_{\theta}/q, plain and truncated at 2. The error is the squared distance for a batch of about 480,000 tokens, on the 1,024 fixed prefixes (64 in parameter space), at the untrained student and steps 100 and 200 of standard runs, for σ=0.0665\sigma=0.0665, 0.15 and 0.325.

Readings.

At σ=0.15\sigma=0.15 and steps 100 and 200, the 95% intervals of the error ratio to plain OPD, at 64 prefixes, leave it undetermined whether truncated weights or score centering on 128 tokens reduce the error. Two of seven predictions, fixed in advance, about the corrections’ per-token variance held.

Whole-response reweighting.

Only reweighting whole responses by pθ/qp_{\theta}/q reaches the prefix shift. Its expected effective fraction is at most exp(−KL(pθ∥q))\exp(-\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta}\|q)) over whole responses; approximating that KL by 7,538 tokens (the mean response length) times the mean per-token KL at the fixed prefixes gives 10−2710^{-27} or smaller even at σ=0.0665\sigma=0.0665: about 102710^{27} responses per effective sample, a population estimate, not a bound.

D.2 A teacher-anchored objective at a fixed prefix

This subsection proves the stationarity statement of Section 6 at one prefix, where qq, pθp_{\theta} and pTp_{T} are the engine’s, trainer’s and teacher’s next-token distributions. With Av=log⁡pT​(v)−log⁡pθ​(v)A_{v}=\log p_{T}(v)-\log p_{\theta}(v) held fixed, as in verl, and a probability ratio of 1, the expected loss gradient is Gq=−𝔼q​[A​∇θ​log⁡pθ]G_{q}=-\mathbb{E}_{q}[A\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}], in parameter space.

Proposition.

For fixed qq, let Jq​(θ)=12​𝔼v∼q​[Av2]J_{q}(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{v\sim q}[A_{v}^{2}], now with AA a function of θ\theta. (i) ∇θJq=Gq\nabla_{\theta}J_{q}=G_{q}. (ii) At pθ=pTp_{\theta}=p_{T}, every sampled token’s update is zero, for every engine. (iii) There, the Hessian of JqJ_{q} in the prefix’s logits zz is B⊤​diag​(q)​BB^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(q)\,B, B=I−𝟏​pT⊤B=I-\mathbf{1}p_{T}^{\top}: positive semidefinite and, if all qv>0q_{v}>0, positive definite except in the direction that adds a constant to every logit.

Proof.

(i) qq and pTp_{T} do not depend on θ\theta, so ∇θJq=𝔼q​[A​∇θA]=Gq\nabla_{\theta}J_{q}=\mathbb{E}_{q}[A\,\nabla_{\theta}A]=G_{q}. (ii) Every Av=0A_{v}=0. (iii) As ∇z​log​pθ​(v)=ev−pθ\nabla_{z}\log p_{\theta}(v)=e_{v}-p_{\theta}, differentiating ∇zJq=−∑vqvAv(ev−pθ)\nabla_{z}J_{q}=-\sum_{v}q_{v}A_{v}(e_{v}-p_{\theta}) again at A=0A=0 leaves ∑vqv​(ev−pT)​(ev−pT)⊤=B⊤​diag​(q)​B\sum_{v}q_{v}(e_{v}-p_{T})(e_{v}-p_{T})^{\top}=B^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(q)\,B, and u⊤​B⊤​diag​(q)​B​u=∑vqv​(uv−pT⊤​u)2≥0u^{\top}B^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(q)\,Bu=\sum_{v}q_{v}(u_{v}-p_{T}^{\top}u)^{2}\geq 0, which, if all qv>0q_{v}>0, is zero only for constant uu. □\square

Scope.

The squared log ratio is the “k2” estimator of the KL (Schulman, 2020). The result needs the trainer’s advantage: with the engine’s, log⁡pT​(v)−log⁡q⁡(v)\log p_{T}(v)-\log q(v), the update at pθ=pTp_{\theta}=p_{T} is zero only if q=pTq=p_{T}. The result holds at one prefix with the engine fixed, so it bounds neither the cost of mismatch nor the budget.

D.3 The prefix shift

This subsection splits the update’s error into the per-token error TT, the only part per-token corrections act on, and the prefix shift SS (Figure 9).

Measurement.

For 64 held-out problems, four responses each come from the standard engine, an independent redraw (a placebo, true shift zero), and the engines with weight noise at σ=0.15\sigma=0.15 (passes in training) and 0.325 (fails). At the untrained student and step 200 of the standard run, the expected per-token update is exact at every prefix. Against the on-policy update at the standard engine’s prefixes, the error splits exactly into TT, the error at the engine’s own prefixes, and SS, the on-policy update’s change when the prefixes move to the engine’s. Sizes are cross-fitted over response halves. Two FP8-cache engines were also measured (the every-layer one’s TT was flagged); only the weight-noise sizes are reported.

Readings.

For weight noise, the shift meets the rule fixed in advance: it exceeds the placebo, carries a fifth or more of the error’s squared size, and from the passing to the failing level grows (paired interval excluding zero) by a larger factor than TT. At the untrained student, relative to the on-policy update, SS rises from 0.098 at σ=0.15\sigma=0.15 to 0.517 at 0.325 (5.3 times) and TT from 0.198 to 0.417 (2.1 times), both increases with intervals excluding zero. The split depends on which change is made first: at the untrained student, SS’s factor is also the larger in the reverse order (21.6 against TT’s 12.8) and in the symmetric split (15.2 against 8.0); at step 200 only the order above favors SS (7.8 against 5.9).

Appendix E Real-Kernel Speed Benchmark

This appendix gives the real-kernel evidence for Section 5.4.

Question and setup.

Does a rollout with vLLM’s own low-precision kernels shorten a step at our training shape, 16 sequences per replica? A vLLM 0.19.1 benchmark without training timed BF16, FP8 weights in verl’s recipe, vLLM’s FP8 cache and both, with and without the draft head (App. G), at 16, 64, 128 and, descriptively, 256 per replica.

Rule, fixed in advance.

A configuration within a fixed mismatch limit passes at a batch size if its speedup in batch time, in the median and on every paired prompt set, reaches the threshold against BF16 with and without the draft head: 1.15 at 16 per replica and 1.30 at 64 and 128, each raised by BF16’s job-to-job spread.

Result.

None passed: within the limit, the best speedups were 1.25 / 1.10 / 1.19 at 16, 64 and 128 per replica, against raised thresholds of 1.43 / 1.37 / 1.38. The cache never filled there (peak use at most 0.71, 0 preemptions); BF16’s cache first filled at 256. Model Optimizer’s recipe was not in this benchmark; Table 11 gives its gain in training. The FP8 cache’s benefit is memory: with the first layer’s KV cache in BF16 it holds 1.93×\times as many tokens as BF16’s, at a real-kernel mismatch of 0.0043 [0.0040, 0.0046] nats/token.

What a faster rollout could buy.

With the draft head, generation and teacher scoring take f=68%f=68\% of a mean 107.5 s step in the pilot’s three 100-step standard runs (App. F); without it, 76% in this study (Table 11). A rollout ss times faster raises the step rate by at most 1/((1−f)+f/s)1/((1-f)+f/s): 1.16×\times for s=1.25s=1.25, never above 3.08×\times.

Memory test, fixed in advance.

At 1,536 sequences per step the BF16 cache fills. Memory is shown if the measured ratio RR of updates per hour beats what FP8’s speed alone predicts, Rnp=1/((1−f)+f/snp)R_{\mathrm{np}}=1/((1-f)+f/s_{\mathrm{np}}), by G=R/Rnp≥1.05G=R/R_{\mathrm{np}}\geq 1.05; ff is this BF16 run’s generation and teacher-scoring share (0.42), snps_{\mathrm{np}} the FP8 cache’s generation speedup without training at this batch, with memory to spare (1.13). For the FP8 cache, Rnp=1.051R_{\mathrm{np}}=1.051 and R=1.111R=1.111, so G=1.057G=1.057: memory is shown (G=1.007G=1.007 at 1,024 per step). Model Optimizer FP8 gets no verdict: no snps_{\mathrm{np}} was measured for it. One run each; repeated runs of one configuration have differed by up to 3.6% in run time.

Without the draft head.

Table 11 reruns four configurations for 30 steps without the draft head: vLLM’s FP8 cache, Model Optimizer FP8 and weights up to 4 versions old give 1.002, 1.266 and 2.008 times BF16’s updates per hour. With the head they give 0.989, 1.079 and 1.643 over the same steps 3–30, as over steps 3–200 (0.990, 1.082, 1.624), so the head, not the shorter window, explains the difference.

Appendix F The Pilot

A 100-step pilot on our 7B student with emulated quantization preceded this study; its results are not reported. Its eight quantized engines trained at mismatches up to 1.47 times their offline estimates, which the admission check’s margin of 1.5 covers (Section 4.3). Six outputs are fixed inputs here: the step-time breakdown of its standard runs (App. E); their mean held-out KL, the step-100 reference (App. B.1); the admission line of 0.41 nats/token (Section 4.3); those ratios; two checkpoints of one standard run (Section 6); and its weight-noise run at σ=0.15\sigma=0.15, the OPD run that GRPO and REINFORCE at that engine are compared with at launch and at step 100 (Section 5.5).

Appendix G Reproducibility

Code and data.

The code is at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd/. It holds the engines and their emulation, the training launcher, the offline estimate, the speed benchmark, the gradient probe, the prefix-shift measurement, the held-out evaluation and the preparation of every dataset. The plan, the per-step logs, the analyzers’ outputs and the scripts that write the numbers and figures will be released after the review.

Software and hardware.

The trainer is verl (Sheng et al., 2025) at commit fbb4b3a8 with FSDP (Zhao et al., 2023); vLLM 0.19.1 (Kwon et al., 2023) with PyTorch 2.10 runs rollouts and the teacher. A synchronous OPD run uses two nodes of four GH200 GPUs, one for the trainer with four rollout replicas and one for the teacher; GRPO and REINFORCE use one. The driver is 595.91.07 with CUDA 13.2; the second runs at 0.097 and 0.39 (Section 5.1), and most likely the FP8 run with weights up to 4 versions old (Figure 6), used 615.71.09.

Models and data.

The 7B student and teacher use revisions 916b56a4 and fcef970f. Every OPD and RL run on this pair decodes rollouts with a public EAGLE-3 draft head (Li et al., 2025b) and 3 draft tokens, except the memory tests and the 30-step runs of Table 11; offline estimates, evaluations and the smaller students use none. Speculative decoding leaves the rollout engine’s distribution unchanged (Leviathan et al., 2023), and every speed comparison pairs runs with the same setting. The head’s published configuration omits max_position_embeddings, so vLLM builds a rotary cache for only 2,048 positions; we set the field to 131,072. Training prompts are DAPO-Math-17k (Yu et al., 2025); the held-out set is AIME24 (MAA, 2024) and MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), including 38 problems flagged as overlapping the training pool.

Training configuration.

Each OPD run takes 200 steps of 8 prompts ×\times 8 samples at temperature 1 without top-pp or top-kk, at most 16,384 response tokens and one AdamW step per batch at a constant learning rate of 10−610^{-6} (weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1.0). The loss is verl’s k1 estimator in policy-gradient form, with the advantage of Eq. (1); task rewards, KL penalties, entropy bonus and rollout importance corrections are off.

Seeds, evaluation and compute.

Seeds are 1 for the data order, 20261001 for the weight noise and, for rollouts, 42 (43 in the second runs at 0.097 and 0.39) plus rr for replica rr; the engine is not deterministic. Every checkpoint is evaluated with the standard engine at temperature 1, up to 16,384 tokens, with evaluation seeds fixed per problem and sample and shared by all runs; a rule checks the last boxed answer. A 200-step synchronous run took 5.5 to 6.0 hours on eight GPUs. Scripts write most numbers in the gradient probe and the benchmark result (App. D and E); the per-run tables were copied by hand.

Appendix I Limitations

We study reverse-KL OPD with the single-sample estimator of Eq. (1), on math.

  • •

    One run per configuration. Intervals resample problems, not runs, so verdicts are provisional; repeated configurations differ by 1.0% and 1.5% in held-out KL (App. B.5). The second runs at 0.097 and 0.39, and most likely the FP8 run with weights up to 4 versions old, used a newer GPU driver without a control run, so that run’s speed ratios include any driver difference (App. G).

  • •

    One main pair. The budget, 0.184 to 0.39 nats/token, is our 7B student’s, and no run lies inside it. Our teacher is an RL fine-tune of the student; a pair farther apart may have a smaller budget. The 1.5B student’s budget is not located, one Llama-3.2-3B run detects only held-out KL rises of 14 to 20% or more, and no training result covers Qwen3, whose 4B student failed our check that plain OPD trains on it.

  • •

    Length, hardware and speed. Runs last at most 200 steps on GH200 GPUs; the noise level whose verdict changed between steps 100 and 200 moved toward failure in both runs. NVFP4 is emulated (quality only). Each FP8 speed gain comes from one short run, and the memory saving’s credit, 5.7%, just passes its 5% bar.

  • •

    Time to quality and admission. With FP8, weights up to 8 versions old reach the synchronous run’s final held-out KL only at the last checkpoint; up to 4 versions old, they end 0.8% above it, within the spread of repeated runs (Table 11). No admission prediction was tested near the budget’s edge (App. B.4).

  • •

    Staleness and RL. Stale-weight runs stay below 0.005 nats/token, so OPD’s staleness limit is not located; GRPO and REINFORCE did not pass our learning test in 200 steps.

  • •

    Mechanism. The fixed prefixes may overstate how much the error shrinks in training: there the KL to the teacher falls 28-fold, against 2-fold for held-out KL. Still open: why noise at 0.39 fails only by step 200, why per-token corrections did not help, and why positive offsets lower held-out KL; the larger offset costs 2.9 points of accuracy [−4.95-4.95, −0.91-0.91].
